text: Most companies adopting Microsoft 365 or Azure already have years of on-premises Active Directory running, and they can't just throw it away. Hybrid identity is how one identity ends up working in both worlds instead of two disconnected ones — and it's the real-world constraint this entire chapter is built around.

That on-prem AD holds the real stakes: every employee's user account, the security groups controlling who can reach a file share or line-of-business app, and Group Policy enforcing password rules and software deployment across the whole company. None of that was built in a weekend, and none of it disappears just because the company signs up for Azure. Rebuilding it from scratch in the cloud would be its own multi-year project.

That leaves two bad options. Stay on-prem only, and nobody can sign into Microsoft 365 or Azure. Abandon on-prem AD for a cloud-only identity, and every app, printer, and Group Policy tied to that directory breaks immediately. Hybrid identity is the real answer: keep on-prem AD exactly as it is, and extend it into the cloud instead of replacing it, so cloud adoption happens gradually instead of all at once.

In practice that means on-premises AD stays the source of truth, where accounts are actually created and managed. A synchronized copy of those objects — users, groups, some attributes — flows into Entra ID on a schedule. The employee signs in with the same corporate username and password whether they're hitting a file server down the hall or Outlook in the cloud, with no second account to create or remember.

That sync mechanism is Microsoft Entra Connect, covered next in Lesson 2 — the tool that actually keeps on-prem AD and Entra ID consistent, and the first real piece of making hybrid identity work. Later lessons build on it: how authentication itself gets verified, and how this same identity story extends to AWS.
